Four principles
for dealing with other cultures

blocks.html:
1. People may not fit the stereotype. Not every American, Japanese or Mexican behaves the same. Know the general culture, but keep your eyes open for the person in front of you.

Cultural

Question The professor’s answer

Four stages of
dealing with a new culture

blocks.html: Imagine you move to a new country for work. What goes on in your mind? Excitement? Fear? Most people pass through four stages.
blocks.text:
Imagine you move to a new country for work. What goes on in your
mind? Excitement? Fear? Most people pass through four
stages .

blocks.alt: Four stages in a new culture
blocks.caption:
Elation, transition,
understanding, integration.

blocks.html:
Stage How it feels What you say
1. Elation Everything is new and exciting. “Wow! Look at that!” “I love this place!” “So many types of chocolate!” “I didn’t know you could drink water straight from the tap.”
2. Transition Frustration, confusion, dissatisfaction. You may want to go home. This is the “complaining” stage. “The food is so bland. Haven’t they heard of spices?” “I don’t even know how to flush.” “Why did that person laugh when I asked for a ticket?” “I keep getting embarrassed.”
3. Understanding Familiarity grows. You start to feel at home. “I’m starting to understand the traffic rules.” “Baseball is a great game. Let’s go this weekend.” “People here are polite. They don’t mind repeating things if I ask.”
4. Integration You accept the differences and adapt. Your old culture may even start to feel a little unfamiliar. “I love sushi.” “I’ll sign up for golf lessons on Friday.” “There must be a reason for their obsession with time.”

tap.” 2. Transition Frustration, confusion, dissatisfaction. You may
want to go home. This is the “complaining” stage. “The food is so bland. Haven’t they heard of spices?” “I don’t even
know how to flush.” “Why did that person laugh when I asked for a
ticket?” “I keep getting embarrassed.” 3. Understanding Familiarity grows. You start to feel at home. “I’m starting to understand the traffic rules.” “Baseball is a great
game. Let’s go this weekend.” “People here are polite. They don’t mind
repeating things if I ask.” 4. Integration You accept the differences and adapt . Your old
culture may even start to feel a little unfamiliar. “I love sushi.” “I’ll sign up for golf lessons on Friday.” “There
must be a reason for their obsession with time.”

Case study: the doctor and
the nurse

blocks.html:
Lecture example — cultural understanding and creativity Situation: A large hospital in the USA. A doctor from Uruguay. A nurse from the Philippines. A machine is attached to every patient in intensive care, and there is a set way to run it.

What went wrong: The doctor explains the machine and leaves. Mistakes happen, and there are many last-minute emergencies. The doctor is upset: “I told you how to do it. Why didn’t you?” The nurse says nothing. Someone tells him she is making mistakes. He asks, “Then why doesn’t she just tell me she doesn’t understand?”

Interpretation: The doctor comes from an equal culture. The nurse comes from an unequal culture. In her culture, you don’t question an older or more educated person. Even if you don’t understand, you keep quiet.

Synergistic solution: The doctor tells her, “It’s okay to ask me doubts.” The nurse says, “Doctor, may I ask some doubts? I don’t mean any disrespect.” Both change a little and work it out together.

One example for each

blocks.html:
Strategy Lecture example
Avoidance A US company’s branch abroad. US rules gave health insurance only to the employee’s wife. Local employees, from a collective culture, also claimed for their children. The company avoided the issue. It never raised a question and simply paid the bills.
Dominance A local partner gives a US partner a small welcome gift. The American refuses: “Accepting gifts is like a bribe in our company.” The partner explains it is only a welcome gift. He still refuses. He won’t budge.
Accommodation A Western businessman goes to Japan to sign a contract. Like India, Japan is relationship-oriented. For about two weeks they only play golf and go out for meals. His boss keeps asking, “Why haven’t you signed yet?” He adjusts to their way: build the relationship first.
Compromise Teams from two countries (say, Italy and Mexico) take turns: meetings in Mexico for two months, then in Italy for two months. They meet midway.
Synergy The Uruguayan doctor and the Filipino nurse: he invites questions, and she asks respectfully.

What is personal grooming?

blocks.text:

blocks.html:
Speaker Their meaning of grooming
Lt Col Jayakumar Parents groom a child, in body and in feelings. At work, it is how you dress, appear, smile, speak and behave with people. It is a kind of social adjustment: fitting into your surroundings in a way society approves of.

How to build the mindset

blocks.html: You will move between jobs, cities and countries, and between a party and a funeral on the same day. How do you adjust?
blocks.text:
You will move between jobs, cities and countries, and between a party
and a funeral on the same day. How do you adjust?

blocks.html:
1. Learn from people around you. At a funeral, watch how your parents speak and behave. At a doctor’s clinic, Prof. Sivakumar got bored waiting and arranged the messy footwear neatly at the door. After that, everyone who came in placed their footwear neatly too. Grooming begets grooming. It spreads like a ripple. Be a role model, or find one.
  2. Change your behaviour to suit the person. You speak differently to an elder, a child, a lady, your boss and your juniors.
  3. Have a hunger to learn. Accept that there is always more to learn: customs, traditions, table manners (many kinds of forks, spoons and glasses). Even the Colonel says he hasn’t learned it all.
  4. Mind the details.
    • Handshake: not a crushing grip, not a weak, limp one. It should feel warm. Adjust it for a child, an elderly person or a lady.
    • Be presentable from head to toe: shirt colour, trousers, sleeve length, shoes, haircut, shave. In the army, officers sometimes shave twice a day, at 4:30 a.m. for PT and again for an evening dinner.
    • Smile. “One smile and your job is done.”
  5. Use structure. A shoe rack at the door tells guests to leave their footwear there without a word. A coat hanger works the same way. Structure guides behaviour.

blocks.text: Culture

blocks.html:
• Culture = shared beliefs, values, norms and practices of a group.
  • It is passed down through generations and guides us subconsciously.
  • We are born into a culture, not born with it. We take it in through socialisation.
  • Notice three kinds of differences: physical (food, water, shops), sensory (sounds, smells, climate) and cultural (customs, manners, gestures).
  • Observe, don’t judge. You don’t have to agree with another culture.
  • Iceberg principle: above the water we see language, food, dress, customs. Below it are work, priorities, time, privacy, communication, problem solving, aggressiveness and process improvement.

Cross-cultural intelligence
